generatedProse.concept-context: The common presentation errors show up in psychology talks as much as anywhere. Reading dense method slides word for word loses the audience; overrunning means the discussion of what a finding means gets rushed; a slide crammed with statistics splits attention from the speaker. Each error is fixable before the day, and the fix is usually less work, not more: fewer words on a slide, one clear figure, a rehearsal to time. Spotting the error is most of the cure.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students give the same presentation on a study to the same seminar group.

Tom has strong material but faces the screen and reads each slide aloud. The slides are full of method detail, the talk runs three minutes over, and the discussion of what the finding means is rushed to make up time. The group follows the slides, not the speaker, and the main point is lost in the overrun. The content deserved better than its delivery.

Amara gives the same content but has checked it against the common errors. The slides are cut to prompts and one clear figure, so the talk is to the audience, not the screen. It has been rehearsed to time, with a point planned to drop if needed, so the conclusion about the finding lands cleanly. The group follows the argument, and the message stays with them.

The material was identical. Only Amara corrected the errors that would otherwise have undone it.
generatedProse.summary: Good psychology content can still be undone by a few common errors: reading the slides, overrunning, overloaded slides, and losing the audience. Each one is fixable before the day, and spotting it is most of the cure. You can now identify these errors, tell them apart from sound delivery choices, and correct them. With a fitting approach, a supporting structure and the errors in check, you are ready to deliver well.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that corrected the errors?

items.text: She cut the slides to prompts and one clear figure, and rehearsed to time with a point to drop.
She added more method detail to the slides so nothing was forgotten.
She spoke faster to fit all the material in.
She faced the screen so the slides could be read in full.

feedback.correct: That's right. Cutting slides to prompts and a clear figure, and rehearsing to time, corrected the errors.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the corrections that fixed the reading and the overrun.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara cut the slides to prompts and one figure and rehearsed to time, with a point to drop. More detail, speaking faster or facing the screen are the errors, not fixes.
